correctness.rationale: Direct score inequalities give an if-and-only-if strict mismatch domain, with reflection producing two disjoint extremes. Exact multinomial weights prove the finite-n formula. Exponential tilting at t=(log 2)/2 has mean-zero span-one increment, variance 2sqrt(2)/(1+2sqrt(2)), and both omitted score constraints have strict tilted slack and exponentially small failure probability. Fourier inversion establishes the lattice local limit and uniform O(1/sqrt(n)) bound, allowing dominated geometric summation and the stated exact prefactor. An independent ordered-ballot enumeration n=1..8 reproduces the compressed formula; the infinite limit is analytical, not inferred from finite checks.

originality.rationale: The full open article of Mousseau–Surugue–Wilczynski, Corollary 10 and Proposition 11, gives asymptotic Walsh agreement and a concentration-derived lower bound but not the exact three-candidate strict two-unique-winner plurality–Borda mismatch probability, sharp exponential rate, or lattice prefactor. Its Proposition 24 treats a different urn culture. The earlier French 2025 version was inspected and contains no equivalent calculation; earlier impartial-culture formulas use a different sampling law. The new formula is not a corollary of the cited bounds, although historical priority remains subject to inaccessible theses and unindexed literature.
residual_risks: A previously derived sharp three-candidate calculation may appear in a thesis, a work not indexed by the consulted services, or a full paper not obtained.
The JIAF 2025 conference dates establish an early public dissemination window, not the precise earliest time a manuscript appeared online.
The present statistic excludes all tie profiles, whereas some prior set-valued agreement definitions count them differently.

value.rationale: The agreement rate between two standard voting rules in a common empirical single-peaked test culture is a motivated statistical object, directly extending recent qualitative agreement work. The exact all-n law, first possible discrepancy at four voters, one-direction structural classification, and sharp decay exponent together provide a quantitative benchmark for election simulation sample sizes and rare-event comparison; the known generic concentration bound does not answer this question. No arbitrary unrelated parameters are introduced.
